 4                          Direct Pro Se Testimony of Stephen Fischmann

 5   Please state your name and address


 6   Stephen Fischmann. 4848 Deadwood Camp Ct., Las Cruces 88011


 7   Who do you represent?


 8   Myself as a pro se intervenor.


 9   What are you testifying about


10   ROE and capital structure.


11   Why are you focusing on these issues?


12   ROE and capital structures have lasting impacts on utility rates and operations that compound over time.

13   The cumulative effects are far greater than what is visible in a single year. EPE’s 10.7% ROE and

14   55.5% equity capital structure proposals are driven by assumptions that defy financial reality and

15   significantly harm ratepayers. I bring significant background in finance and in utility regulation to this

16   subject.

                                                          1
 17   Please summarize your educational and professional experience


18   I graduated with an MBA from UCLA’s Anderson School of Business in 1979 with concentrations in

19   finance and marketing. I subsequently worked at Levi Strauss and Company from 1979 to 2000 in a

20   variety of positions including Planning Analyst for the Menswear Division, Controller for Subsidiary

21   Santone Industries, Controller for Levi’s designer group, Operations Manager for Levi’s Designer

22   Group, President of Levi’s Designer Group, Director of Finance and Planning for the Women’s Wear

23   Division, and Director of the Supplier Relations initiative of supply chain re-engineering for Levi’s

24   corporate. In those roles I served as the lead analyst for several business acquisitions and divestments

25   and helped negotiate various licensing agreements. From 2000-2005 I operated property inspection and

26   Real Estate Brokerage businesses before retiring to New Mexico. I served in the New Mexico Senate,

27   District 37 where I was a member of the Conservation Committee and chaired the Science and

28   Technology interim committee from 2009-2012. Most utility-related legislation and policy was

29   reviewed in those committees. I was an elected member and rotating chair of the Public Regulation

30   Commission (PRC) from 2019-2022. I have been an advocate on energy issues since 2006, serving on

31   various energy, and environmental nonprofit boards and committees including the Southwest Energy

32   Alliance, CCAE, CVNM, and the Coalition of Sustainable Communities. I have also been an advocate

33   against predatory lending co-chairing the New Mexico Fair Lending Coalition and the New Mexico

34   Consumer Protection Alliance.


35   Are you sponsoring any Witnesses?


36   Yes. I am co-sponsoring Mark Ellis along with CCAE. Mark currently works with Market Clear where

37   he has become a nationally recognized expert on ROE and its impact on fair, just and reasonable rates.




                                                         2
 38   Mr. Ellis will explain the core ideas and assumptions required to develop a realistic ROE and capital

39   structure.


40   Will there be significant overlap between your testimony and Mr. Ellis’?


41   No. I will present a big picture overview, while Mr. Ellis dives into specific ROE and capital structure

42   recommendations.


43   What is the legal standard for establishing utility ROEs in rates.


44   Bluefield Water Works & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S.

45   679 (1923) sets a clear standard.


46   "A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the value of the property
47   which it employs for the convenience of the public equal to that generally being made at the same time
48   and in the same general part of the country on investments in other business undertakings which are
49   attended by corresponding risks and uncertainties; but it has no constitutional right to such profits as
50   are realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures."

51   The clear intent is to benchmark a utilities returns to market returns on investments with corresponding

52   risks. This provides an objective and visible basis for setting profit awards that balance investor and

53   ratepayer interests. Other regulated utilities have traditionally been the benchmark companies in U.S.

54   ratemaking proceedings.


55   What concerns do you have about EPE’s proposed ROE?


56   EPE’s 10.7% proposal is nearly twice as high as current returns in the capital markets on utility

57   investments. This is grossly out of step with Bluefield, and the common regulatory adage that utility

58   ROEs should be high enough to attract capital, but no higher. Table 1 below documents annual ROE

59   across US electric utilities since 2010 using NYU Stern Publicly available data.

 67   Why are market ROEs so much lower than regulator awarded ROEs?


68   Investors correctly assess that regulated utility profits are so reliable that minimal risk premiums are

69   required. When regulators award 9.5% to 10.5% returns on book value, competitive markets quickly

70   determine that investments of equivalent risk (generally other utilities) typically earn 5-6% on market

71   value. Stock prices are bid up above book value bringing their returns in line with the rest of the utility

72   market.


73   The phenomenon is comparable to what would happen in bond markets. If the market return on risk-

74   free 30- year debt is 5% and someone floats a risk- free $1 million bond with a 10% interest rate, the

75   market bids the bond price up to about $2 million. This occurs because the returns mimic a $2 million

76   dollar bond earning the market rate.


77   The question is not whether utilities can raise equity for well under 10.7%. They already do. The

78   question is whether utilities should charge customers their actual cost of capital as outlined in Bluefield,

79   or rely on traditionally misapplied theoretical formulas to collect massive markups on the cost of capital.


80   Are inflated ROE awards a temporary phenomenon?


81   No. As shown in table 1 above, this has been going for many years. Utilities across the country have

82   been awarded 9-11% returns while the equity markets continue to require only 5-6%.         Ratepayers have

83   been footing the bill for nearly twice the market cost of capital.


84   Why are investors content with modest returns on utility stocks?


85   Investor-owned utilities are among the safest equity investments in the marketplace. The customer base

86   is guaranteed through regional monopolies. Regulators are required to award reasonable profits during

87   rate cases. Significant variable costs such as fuel and contracted power are passed directly to the
                                                           5
  88   consumer’s bill. When an unforeseeable expense occurs, utilities can petition regulators for emergency

 89   relief. Utility investment risk is so low that equity investors are satisfied with returns equivalent to some

 90   investment grade bonds.


 91   Do you anticipate future developments that justify awarded ROE’s 4-5% above recent market
 92   ROEs?

 93   I do not. The stability of market ROEs over time indicatse investors don’t either. The permanence of

 94   IOU regulatory structures and the protections of government rate setting place regulated utilities in an

 95   entirely different risk category than typical equities. Risk, as measured by beta, will remain well below

 96   equity market averages unless core industry characteristics radically change.


 97   Are profits a source of capital for grid improvement and expansion?

 98   No. Profits are an almost non-existent source of capital expansion funds for the typical IOU. EEI data

 99   shows an average of 60-70% of IOU profit goes to investor dividends. Another 20- 25% goes to federal

100   and state taxes. EPE witness Richard Gonzalez’ testimony confirms that EPE paid IIF US 2 $461.8

101   million in common dividends from 2022-2024, representing slightly more than 100% of total reported

102   income for the period. This is confirmed by FERC form 1 reporting in accounts 438 and 216.


103   Are regulator established ROEs developed based on utility market returns?


104   No. Regulatory returns are established through testimony, comparison to awarded ROEs in other

105   jurisdictions, and DCF and CAPM modeling. There is no direct benchmarking to actual utility ROEs as

106   required by Bluefield. Because the fallback benchmark in practice is awarded ROEs at other utilities, an

107   industry feedback loop has been created that has pushed ROE awards far above required investor returns

108   (cost of equity) in the real world.




                                                           6
 109   Utility modeling engages in extensive analysis of historic and largely irrelevant data to justify DCF and

110   CAPM formula assumptions. It has become an elaborate Rube Goldberg exercise that conceals the true

111   cost of equity with misapplied economic theory and circular reasoning. It ignores the most important

112   and timely data – contemporaneous utility market returns. ROE awards based on modelling from a

113   limited number of rate case intervenors have consistently exceeded annual investor returns by 60% to

114   120%. The process unfairly penalizes ratepayers and defeats the balancing of interests required by the

115   PUA in 62-3-1-b NMSA1. Awarded ROEs will remain inflated until they are benchmarked to utility

116   equity markets as originally outlined in Bluefield.


117   Why should we trust market valuations more than regulatory ROE formulas?


118   Utility equity is 70-90 percent owned by sophisticated institutional investors based on AI aggregated

119   SEC form 13F and schedule 13G filings. Vanguard, Blackrock, State Street, and pension funds are

120   among the primary shareholders. They evaluate markets deeply and continuously. They understand risk

121   and opportunity costs, and they have outstanding access to market information. They invest based on

122   anticipated future profits. That means their required forward-looking return, cost of equity, is baked into

123   a market price they strongly influence.


124   Contemporaneous utility stock market valuations, driven by sophisticated institutional investors, have

125   proven vastly superior to regulatory modeling at predicting required investor returns. That makes sense.

126   Investors are the market. Utility executives and regulators can only pretend to be the market.


127   Will a significant reduction in ROE violate gradualism principles?


128   EPE’s proposed 50% rate increase just 6 years after its last rate case shows no regard for gradualism

129   principles. If dramatic rate increases are on the table, dramatic awarded ROE reductions should be as

130   well. Ratepayers have been overcharged on ROE for decades. While past overpayments cannot be
                                                      7
 131   recovered, there is no excuse for allowing them to continue. The proposed rate increase requires

132   regulators to examine all reasonable cost mitigation measures. A significant downward adjustment of

133   ROE in these circumstances serves the principle of rate setting gradualism.


134   When do we know awarded ROE correctly balances investor and ratepayer interests?

135   When market to book value ratios fall in the range of 95-115%. At those levels, ratepayers don’t pay

136   premiums that serve solely to goose up stock prices, and utility investors continue to earn a fair market

137   tested rate of return. Table 2 below shows significantly elevated market to book value ratios across the

138   US electric utility industry since 2010. Valuations high above book value mean the market recognizes

139   profits exceed required returns for the investment. It is a proof statement that awarded profits favor

140   companies and investors over ratepayers.

155   Ms. Nelson’s amended testimony exhibit 9 on behalf of EPE shows an aggregate Market to Book Value

156   ratios of 2.1 for her proxy companies -presumably at the date of filing.


157   Is maintaining enterprise valuation or stock price a concern of the commission?


158   Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591 (1944)2makes clear that it is not.

159   Market values are an outcome of a regulatory process focused on fair, just, and reasonable rates.




                                                          9
 160   Presupposing fair enterprise valuations puts the cart before the horse by effectively dictating revenue

161   requirements independent of the required analysis of fair, just, and reasonable rates.


162   You have shown that a 10.7% ROE greatly exceeds the Bluefield Standard. Will your
163   recommended return enable EPE to maintain its financial integrity, attract capital, and
164   compensate investors for the risks assumed?

165   Yes. These issues are addressed in answers to the questions that follow.


166   Will individual investors be badly harmed by a significant drop in awarded ROE?


167   EPE’s market value likely will decline to some degree, but everybody holding an ownership interest

168   does so through the diversified IIF US 2 investment fund. EPE represents a small portion of that fund so

169   no investor will suffer significant degradation of their total investment. Since the fund caters to large

170   investors who are generally well diversified already, the impact on their overall portfolio will be further

171   diluted. The main point here is that no investor will find themselves out on the street because EPE lost

172   market value. The same holds true for other New Mexico IOUs. Online stock analysis platforms such

173   as Yahoo Finance, ChartMill and Market Beat estimate Excel, the holding company for SPS, is 80-90%

174   owned by institutions. Estimates of TXNM institutional ownership range from 91-100%.


175   Could reduced ROE awards dry up capital availability by pushing investors to utilities awarded
176   higher ROEs?

177   Only temporarily until the dust settles. But generally, no. As previously noted, utility equity investors

178   have established a national market for regulated utility returns clustered around annual ROEs of 5-6%.

179   EPE’s market valuation will adjust to reward new investors at the same level and IIF US 2 fund share

180   prices will adjust to attract capital as they always have. Awarding ROEs far above the market cost of

181   equity does not attract needed capital. It only overcharges ratepayers for capital that is already

182   available..

                                                          10
 183   Could reduced ROE result in under investment in necessary grid maintenance, upgrades and
184   expansion?

185   EPE failed in its appeal of a 9% ROE award in its last rate case. Since that decision, EPE’s New Mexico

186   capital spending rate has far exceeded peak demand growth rates in the New Mexico jurisdiction – a

187   whopping $408 million of new investment according to this rate filing. Over investment rather than under

188   investment is the real concern.


189   A recent research paper from the UC Berkeley Energy Institute entitled “Rate of Return Revisited”

190   found “Higher regulated returns incentivize utilities to own more capital: a one percentage point rise in

191   return on equity corresponds to an increase in capital assets of 2%–4%. 3 If this analysis is accurate, a

192   3% reduction in ROE would reduce capital account balances by about 9% over time.


193   Awarding excessive ROEs in response to a perceived threat of underinvestment puts regulators in the

194   position of succumbing to the monopoly profiteering they are charged with preventing. Throwing rate

195   payers under the bus is not the appropriate response. Regulatory vigilance is.


196   How will lower ROE awards impact credit ratings?


197   Maintaining investment grade credit ratings is crucial for utilities to have access to the debt they need.

198   Reduced ROE will impact the Funds from Operations (FFO) metric relied upon by credit rating

199   agencies. The primary tool to address this issue is a shift in capital structure. More equity and less debt

200   can restore FFO metrics to investment grade levels when necessary.


201   Because a significant portion of FFO comes from depreciation and amortization expense, and because

202   the gap between market-based ROE and debt financing costs is small compared to the gap between

203   regulator calculated ROE and debt, the cost of this capital structure shift will be many times lower than

204   the savings from reduced ROE.

                                                           11
 205   An analysis of capital structures that most economically meet financing and credit rating requirements at

206   given ROEs is far more useful for fair rate setting than arbitrary adoption of potentially manipulated

207   capital ratios on the books at the time of rate filings.


208   What other impacts might reduced ROE’s have on EPE operations?.


209   At our proposed level, predictable impacts include an approximate 10% near- term reduction in

210   customer rates, stronger cost controls, and more rigorous evaluation of future investments. Based on

211   information from this proceeding, these are positive impacts in what appears to be an extravagant capital

212   spending environment.


213   Does a market-based ROE endanger EPE’s financial stability?


214   It does not. Current EPE profits go to dividends and taxes. There will be limited impact on available

215   operating funds. Straightforward adjustments to capital structure will preserve investment grade credit

216   ratings. Profits, though lower, are still largely protected. Given the reliability of utility revenues,

217   competent management should have few issues maintaining a stable enterprise generating fair investor

218   returns.


219   Is there broader recognition of the need for utility ROE reforms?

220   Academics and policy makers are waking up to the reality that awarded 10% returns to low-risk

221   regulated utilities are out of step with actual investor expectations and fair treatment of ratepayers. The

222   previously cited UC Berkely Energy Institute Rate of Regulatory Return Revisited study shows ROE

223   awards ranging from 2% to 4% above reasonable investment markers over time.




                                                            12
 224   The Bluefield decision is clear that monopoly utilities are not entitled to high profits earned by

225   commercial enterprises facing competition. “A public utility……. has no constitutional right to such

226   profits as are realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures."


227   Rapidly rising costs and massive utility investment have made utility bills a national issue. Policy

228   makers are finally acting. Pennsylvania bill HB2224 requiring ROEs fixed at 2% above 10-year

229   treasury rates or alternative market- based ROEs passed the House by a vote of 202-0. Similar

230   legislation has been introduced in both New York legislative Chambers: Assembly Bill A11197 and

231   Senate Bill S10424. California recently enacted AB 2463. It puts strict procedures in place to better

232   analyze utility business risk and contain ROE cost. The governors of Pennsylvania, Illinois, and New

233   York have publicly advocated for reigning in utility costs. New Mexico will not be an outlier by

234   addressing this issue.


235   What are your recommendations for EPE ROE and capital structure?


236   The statistical relationship between market based utility ROEs and contemporaneous US treasuries has

237   proven durable over time. The most straightforward way to establish ROEs in rates is to add the historic

238   spread between treasuries and utility annual returns to recent treasury rates. This eliminates gaming of

239   CAPM and DCF models while keeping a firm connection to real world investor minimum required

240   returns.


241   I’ve used a 5% 30 year treasury rate and a five year average of the treasury to utility return spread for

242   the purposes of this recommendation. Forecasts of future interest rates should not be used because they

243   have proved dramatically inaccurate across the financial industry. Appendix B shows market utility

244   returns have consistently hovered 0-2% above ten year treasuries throughout the 2020s. Given that

245   history, I recommend an ROE between 6.5% and 7.5%. See appendix B for the calculations.

                                                          13
 246   I cannot recommend a capital structure until an FFO analysis is performed to confirm what is required

247   to maintain investment grade credit ratings. Such analysis should be required as part of any utility rate

248   submission in the future. In EPE’s case, I would not be surprised to see a 60% equity ratio at a 7%

249   ROE. As my witness Mr. Ellis will show, the increased equity ratio will have only minor impacts on the

250   overall rate savings.

253   investors require the regulation and supervision of public utilities to the end that reasonable and proper services shall

255   attracted so as to provide for the construction, development and extension, without unnecessary duplication and
256   economic waste, of proper plants and facilities and demand-side resources for the rendition of service to the general
257   public and to industry.

258   2) 315 U.S. p. 315 U. S. 582. Ratemaking is indeed but one species of price-fixing. Munn v. Illinois, 94 U. S. 113, 94 U.

260   being regulated. But the fact that the value is reduced does not mean that the regulation is invalid. Block v. Hirsh, 256

262   indicate that "fair value" is the end product of the process of ratemaking, not the starting point, as the Circuit Court of
263   Appeals held. The heart of the matter is that rates cannot be made to depend upon "fair value" when the value of the
264   going enterprise depends on earnings under whatever rates may be anticipated.
